title: "Getting and running the code"

## Getting the code {#getting-the-code}

The whole project is in one GitHub repository:

**<https://github.com/BasBBakkerIMF/OpenAI-API-convert-charts>**

You can browse the files on that page. To work with them, clone the repository to your machine:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/BasBBakkerIMF/OpenAI-API-convert-charts.git
cd OpenAI-API-convert-charts
```

If you don't use git, choose **Code → Download ZIP** on the GitHub page and unzip it.

## What is in the repository {#directory-structure}

```text
OpenAI-API-convert-charts/
│
│   ── The pipeline: scripts you run, in this order ──
├── 1_map_drives.py                              Step 1: map K: and L:
├── 2_export_pictures_from_file_locator.py       Step 2: save the published chart pictures
├── 3_create_chart_list.py                       Step 3: copy the chart list from the File Locator
├── 4_read_all_chart_data_and_put_in_excel.py    Step 4: extract each chart's data
├── 5_create_stems_file.py                       Step 5: write the list of charts to convert
├── 6_generate_r_code_for_charts.py              Step 6: ask the AI model for R code (contains the prompt)
├── 7_create_runall.py                           Step 7: write runall.R
│
│   ── Used by the scripts; you don't run these yourself ──
├── helper_for_4_read_data_from_excel_chart_and_export.py   Reads a chart's data (step 4)
├── helper_for_6_imf_openai_helper.py            Connects to the IMF API gateway (step 6)
├── helper_for_6_home_openai.py                  Connects directly to OpenAI (step 6, alternative)
├── example.txt                                  House-style example R code sent to the model
│
│   ── Produced by the pipeline (October 2026 results) ──
├── chart-list.xlsx                              Step 3: where each chart lives
├── stems.txt                                    Step 5: the charts to convert
├── excel_and_png/                               Steps 2 and 4: one pair per chart
│   ├── fig-2-3.png                                the published picture
│   ├── fig-2-3.xlsx                               the chart's data
│   └── ...
├── r_code/                                      Steps 6 and 7
│   ├── fig-2-3.R                                  generated R code for one chart
│   ├── ...
│   ├── runall.R                                   runs all chart scripts
│   ├── r_code.Rproj                               RStudio project for running the charts
│   └── figures/
│       ├── fig-2-3.png                            the chart as drawn by R
│       └── ...
│
│   ── Set-up ──
├── install.ps1                                  Creates the Python environment
├── requirements.txt                             Python packages needed
├── generate_requirements.py                     Rebuilds requirements.txt from the scripts
├── .gitignore                                   Files git should ignore (including .env)
│
│   ── Documentation ──
├── docs/                                        This book (Quarto source)
├── README.md
├── CLAUDE.md                                    Notes for the Claude Code AI assistant
├── installation-instructions.docx               Certificate set-up on IMF machines
│
└── archive/                                     Earlier versions, kept for reference; not used
```

Three things are worth knowing:

- **The "Produced by the pipeline" files are overwritten when you run the pipeline** with `K:` pointing at this folder. See [If you run the pipeline yourself](#run-yourself).
- **The stem links everything.** For any chart, `excel_and_png/<stem>.png`, `excel_and_png/<stem>.xlsx`, `r_code/<stem>.R` and `r_code/figures/<stem>.png` belong together.
- **Not every chart is complete.** A chart with a picture but no data file, or with R code but no figure, did not make it through every step. If generation failed, step 6 leaves `r_code/<stem>_error.txt` in place of `<stem>.R`.

What you do **not** get is the `.env` file with credentials. It is deliberately left out of the repository, so you need to create your own (see [Set-up](#set-up)).

## The repository includes the results

Besides the code, the repository contains the **inputs and outputs of the October 2026 run**:

- `excel_and_png/`: the published chart image (`<stem>.png`) and extracted data (`<stem>.xlsx`) for every chart;
- `r_code/`: the generated R script for every chart (`<stem>.R`), `runall.R`, and the figures they produce in `r_code/figures/`;
- `chart-list.xlsx` and `stems.txt`: the working lists from steps 3 and 5.

**If you only want the R charts, you don't need Python or the AI model at all.** The generated R scripts read their data from `K:/excel_and_png/` and save to `K:/r_code/figures/`. To run them:

1. Map `K:` to the cloned folder (see [step 1](step-1-map-drives.qmd)), or simply run in a Windows command prompt:

   ```text
   subst K: C:\path\to\OpenAI-API-convert-charts
   ```

2. In R, run one chart with `source("K:/r_code/fig-2-3.R")`, or all of them with `source("K:/r_code/runall.R")`.

## If you run the pipeline yourself, use different directories {#run-yourself}

Every step writes to fixed locations under `K:`. If `K:` points at the cloned repository, running the pipeline **overwrites the files that came with it**: the extracted data, the generated R code and the figures. You then lose the reference results to compare against, and git shows every file as changed.

So write your own run to separate directories. The easiest way is to keep the repository and the working files apart:

1. Create an empty working folder, e.g. `C:\reo-charts-work`.
2. Copy `example.txt` from the repository into it. Step 6 reads it from `K:`.
3. In `1_map_drives.py`, point `K:` at the working folder instead of the repository, and run it.
4. Run the Python scripts from the repository folder as usual. That is also where your `.env` file goes.

All outputs (`chart-list.xlsx`, `stems.txt`, `excel_and_png/`, `r_code/`) are then created in the working folder. The repository's copies stay untouched.

If you'd rather keep `K:` as it is, change the output paths in the scripts instead:

| Script | Settings that point to `K:` |
|---|---|
| `2_export_pictures_from_file_locator.py` | `out_dir` |
| `3_create_chart_list.py` | `output_file` |
| `4_read_all_chart_data_and_put_in_excel.py` | `chart_list_file`, `output_directory` |
| `5_create_stems_file.py` | `chart_list_file`, `stems_file` |
| `6_generate_r_code_for_charts.py` | `example_file`, `stems_file`, `chart_dir`, `output_dir` |
| `7_create_runall.py` | `chart_list_file`, `output_directory`, and the `K:/r_code/` path written into `runall.R` |

## Set-up {#set-up}

To run the pipeline you need:

- **Python**, with the project's packages. In PowerShell, in the repository folder, run `.\install.ps1`. This creates a [virtual environment](appendix-glossary.qmd) in `.venv` and installs everything in `requirements.txt`. Activate it in each new PowerShell window with `.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1`.
- **Access to the AI model**, through a `.env` file in the repository folder. See [Creating the `.env` file](#env-file) below.
- **Access to the REO chart folder** on the shared drive, which step 1 maps to `L:`.
- **R** with `readxl`, `ggplot2`, `dplyr`, `tidyr` and `patchwork`, to run the generated scripts.

On IMF machines, Python must trust the IMF's own security certificate before it can reach the model. The scripts handle this with the `truststore` package. If you still get certificate errors, see `installation-instructions.docx` in the repository.

## Creating the `.env` file {#env-file}

Step 6 needs credentials to reach the AI model. These are kept in a small text file called `.env` in the repository folder, not in the scripts. That way they are never put on GitHub: the repository's `.gitignore` excludes `.env`, so git ignores the file.

### What it looks like

The file has one setting per line, in the form `NAME=value`, with no spaces around the `=` and no quotes.

**For the IMF API gateway** (the default), it contains four settings:

```text
API_KEY=your-api-key
CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
TENANT_ID=your-tenant-id
API_URL=https://the-gateway-address
```

Replace each value on the right with your own. You receive these values when you are given access to the IMF API gateway. All four are required.

**For direct OpenAI access** (e.g. working from home with a personal OpenAI account), it contains one setting:

```text
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
```

To use it, also change the import at the top of `6_generate_r_code_for_charts.py`:

```python
# from helper_for_6_imf_openai_helper import get_client
from helper_for_6_home_openai import get_client
```

A single `.env` file can hold both sets of settings. Each helper reads only the ones it needs.

### How to create it

The file name is exactly `.env`: nothing before the dot, and no `.txt` at the end. Windows Notepad adds `.txt` unless you prevent it, so the easiest way is from PowerShell, in the repository folder:

```powershell
notepad .env
```

Notepad asks whether to create the file. Choose **Yes**, paste the lines above with your own values, and save.

To check that the name is right:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Force .env
```

This should list a file called `.env`. If it says the file cannot be found, the file was probably saved as `.env.txt`. Rename it with `Rename-Item .env.txt .env`.

### Where it must be

Put `.env` in the **repository folder**, next to `6_generate_r_code_for_charts.py`, and **run the scripts from that folder**. The IMF helper looks for `.env` in the folder you run Python from.

### If something is wrong

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Missing required config key: API_KEY` (or `CLIENT_ID`, …) | `.env` was not found, or one of the four lines is missing or misspelt |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY was not found. Add it to the .env file.` | Using the direct-OpenAI helper without `OPENAI_API_KEY` in `.env` |
| A browser window opens asking you to sign in | Normal on the first run with the IMF gateway. After you sign in, it is remembered |

## For a new REO edition

The file names and the edition are written into the scripts. For a new edition, update:

- the `L:` target in step 1 (the new chart folder);
- the File Locator file name and sheet name (e.g. `"October 2026"`) in steps 2 and 3;
- the figure column name (e.g. `"October 2026 REO Figure"`) in steps 3 and 4.

Then run steps 1–7 in order. Each step's page explains what to check.
